LR: Coding-Decoding||phrase coding (2-le.m: Treat each word as a set of the phrases it appears in. A word that appears in exactly the same phrases as a code appears in coded phrases must carry that code. Words that share the same phrase-pattern cannot be told apart, so aim for words whose pattern is unique.
LR: Coding-Decoding||phrase coding (2-le.w: Assuming the code order follows the word order – in these questions the order is scrambled.

LR: Data Sufficiency||arrangement suffic.m: Count the arrangements allowed by each statement separately, then together. A statement is sufficient only if every arrangement it permits gives the same answer to the question.
LR: Data Sufficiency||arrangement suffic.w: Declaring a statement sufficient because one arrangement works. It must work for all that the statement allows.

LR: Direction Sense||multi-turn displace.m: Put the start at (0, 0), track east/north components leg by leg, and use Pythagoras for the straight-line distance. A left turn from north faces west; a right turn from north faces east.
LR: Direction Sense||multi-turn displace.w: Turning relative to north each time instead of relative to the current heading.

LR: Linear & Circular Seating||two-row s.m: Remember that rows facing opposite directions reverse 'left' and 'right'. Draw two rows of boxes, place the fixed clues (ends, opposite pairs) first, then apply 'immediate left' with the correct direction for each row.
LR: Linear & Circular Seating||two-row s.w: Using the same left–right direction for both rows. Row 1 facing south has left = east; row 2 facing north has left = west.

LR: Number & Letter Series||exam-style n.m: Take first differences; if they are not constant take the differences of differences or check ratios. Common patterns: differences doubling, squares/cubes, ×k + n, interleaved series.
LR: Number & Letter Series||exam-style n.w: Stopping at the first pattern that fits two terms. Check it against all the given terms.

LR: Number & Letter Series||letter-numbe.m: Treat each letter position and the number as separate series. Letters usually move by a fixed or growing step in the alphabet; numbers follow their own arithmetic or geometric pattern.
LR: Number & Letter Series||letter-numbe.w: Looking for one rule for the whole cluster, or moving the letters in the wrong direction.

LR: Ranking & Ordering||ranking – counti.m: Translate 'only k scored more than X' to X's exact rank (k + 1) and 'only k scored less' to X's rank from the bottom. 'More than k between' only gives a minimum gap, so use it to eliminate positions.
LR: Ranking & Ordering||ranking – counti.w: Reading 'more than 3 between' as exactly 3, or forgetting that ranks may be fixed from both ends.

LR: Scheduling & Days||weekly schedule –.m: Number the days 1–7 and use 'exactly k before/after' clues to fix positions first. 'More than k exams between' limits how close two exams can be.
LR: Scheduling & Days||weekly schedule –.w: Counting the endpoints themselves when counting the people between two positions.

VARC: Grammar - Sentence Completion & Us.m: Test each word by its job in the sentence: adjectives modify nouns, adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs.
VARC: Grammar - Sentence Completion & Us.w: Calling a word an adverb because it ends in -ly or an adjective because it comes before a noun without checking what it modifies.

VARC: Grammar - Sentence Completion & Us.m: Look for fixed pairs (scarcely … when, no sooner … than, not only … but also) and the tense each demands, then check inversion.
Check what the opening phrase or comparison attaches to. A comparison must be between like things and a participial phrase must describe the subject that follows.
VARC: Grammar - Sentence Completion & Us.w: Fixing grammar locally while leaving a dangling modifier or an illogical comparison.

VARC: Grammar - Sentence Completion & Us.m: Identify the time relationship between the two events: the earlier one in the past perfect, the later in the simple past; add continuous if it was in progress.
VARC: Grammar - Sentence Completion & Us.w: Using the simple past for both actions when one clearly precedes the other.

VARC: Grammar - Sentence Completion & Us.m: Check agreement with the nearer subject for 'neither … nor', preposition choice, and countable/uncountable words (fewer vs less).
VARC: Grammar - Sentence Completion & Us.w: Fixing only the first error you spot when several are possible.

VARC: Idioms & Phrases||idiom meaning.m: Replace the underlined phrase by the literal meaning and see which idiom conveys it. Rule out idioms whose literal meaning is opposite or unrelated.
VARC: Idioms & Phrases||idiom meaning.w: Picking an idiom because one of its words matches the sentence (e.g. 'horse', 'stone') rather than its meaning.

VARC: Para Jumbles - Sentence Ordering||.m: Find the opening sentence (it introduces the topic with no back-reference), then chain sentences using linkers (however, therefore, in other words) and pronouns (these, such). Test the final sequence by reading it through.
VARC: Para Jumbles - Sentence Ordering||.w: Choosing the sentence that merely sounds like an introduction when it contains a pronoun that refers back.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.m: The central theme must cover the whole passage, not one paragraph. Reject options that are too narrow, too broad, or bring in outside ideas.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.w: Choosing an option that is true but covers only part of the passage.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.m: Locate the exact sentence in the passage and match the wording. The right option restates it; wrong ones twist or exaggerate it.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.w: Choosing an option that is true in general but not stated in the passage.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.m: An inference must follow necessarily from the passage with no extra assumptions. Eliminate options that go beyond or contradict the text.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.w: Choosing the option you agree with rather than the one the passage supports.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.m: Summarise the passage in one line before looking at the options, then pick the closest. The main idea covers the beginning, development and conclusion.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.w: Choosing an example the author uses instead of the point the example illustrates.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.m: Identify the underlying principle of the passage, then choose the situation that embodies the same principle, not the one with the same surface features.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.w: Matching on topic (e.g. money, trees) instead of on the structure of the problem.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.m: A good summary keeps the main claim and its key support, in the passage's proportion. Reject options that add claims or drop the conclusion.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.w: Choosing an option that is accurate but leaves out the author's conclusion.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.m: Look at the evaluative words the author uses (e.g. 'merely', 'however', 'unfortunately'). Choose the option that matches the strength of the attitude.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.w: Selecting an extreme tone (angry, delighted) when the author is measured.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.m: Replace the word in the sentence with each option and see which preserves the sense. The meaning here may differ from the common meaning.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.w: Choosing the dictionary's most familiar meaning without testing it in the passage.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.m: First state the passage's claim and the reasoning behind it. The best weakener attacks the link between the evidence and the conclusion (or offers a rival explanation); it is not merely a different fact on the topic.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC (exam-le.w: Picking a statement that is unfavourable in tone but does not actually challenge the argument.

VARC: Vocabulary - Antonyms||advanced vo.m: First fix the meaning of the word in the sentence, then look for the opposite idea. Beware synonyms and near-opposites placed as distractors.
VARC: Vocabulary - Antonyms||advanced vo.w: Choosing a synonym because it 'feels' related to the word.

VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||adv.m: Use the sentence for clues (contrast words like 'despite', 'yet' and consequences). Break the word into root parts if you don't recognise it.
VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||adv.w: Choosing the option that sounds close in spelling or sound.

VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||ant.m: Pin down the sense in the sentence, then pick the opposite. Check that the option is a word, not just a related idea.
VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||ant.w: Choosing a synonym or an unrelated negative word.

VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||col.m: Read the whole sentence for tone: the blanks must agree with one another and with the surrounding clues.
VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||col.w: Filling blanks one at a time without checking that the whole sentence is consistent.

VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||nua.m: Look for a clue word that signals contrast or agreement ('deceptively', 'but', 'although') and choose the word that completes it.
VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||nua.w: Choosing a word that fits the first half but clashes with the second.

VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||syn.m: Substitute each option into the sentence and keep the one that preserves the meaning.
VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||syn.w: Choosing a word that is a general synonym but does not fit this context.

VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||ton.m: Identify the attitude conveyed by the key phrase (praise, irony, contempt). Choose the word with the same attitude and strength.
VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||ton.w: Choosing a word with the right sign (positive/negative) but the wrong strength.

VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||usa.m: Check each sentence for the exact meaning of the word; only one will use it correctly. Rule out sentences where it is used for a different but similar-sounding word.
VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||usa.w: Accepting a sentence because the word 'sounds' right.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||centroid w.m: Centroid = average of the three vertices, so set each coordinate of the average equal to the given point and solve the resulting equations for the unknowns. Substitute back to answer what is asked.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||centroid w.w: Averaging only two vertices, or dividing by 2 instead of 3. Check the final point satisfies every given condition.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||chord of a.m: Length of a chord = 2√(r² − d²), where d is the perpendicular distance of the centre from the line (d = |ax₀ + by₀ + c| ÷ √(a² + b²)). Find d first, then the chord.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||chord of a.w: Using the radius or the diameter directly, or forgetting the factor 2 (the formula gives the half-chord).

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||reflection.m: Reflect P in ax + by + c = 0 using (x′, y′) = (x, y) − 2(ax + by + c)/(a² + b²) · (a, b). Check: the midpoint of P and P′ lies on the line and PP′ is perpendicular to it.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||reflection.w: Sign errors in (ax + by + c) – compute it once and reuse it for both coordinates.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||triangle f.m: Find the three vertices by solving the lines pairwise, then use the shoelace formula ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|. Verify each vertex lies on both of its lines.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||triangle f.w: Assuming a right angle or a nice shape without checking slopes; losing the ½ in the area.

Algebra: Functions||additive functional.m: Substitute y = 1 (or another small value) to turn the equation into a recursion for f(x + 1) in terms of f(x), then sum the recursion from x = 1 up to the required value, using the given f(1).
Algebra: Functions||additive functional.w: Dropping the cross term (such as −2xy) when summing – it changes with x and must be added up separately.

Algebra: Functions||composition with pie.m: Evaluate from the inside out. For each stage, first decide which branch of the piecewise rule applies to the current value, then compute.
Algebra: Functions||composition with pie.w: Using the same branch at every stage. After each step the input has changed, so re-check which region it falls in.

Algebra: Functions||floor × polynomial d.m: List every point where the floor function jumps (e.g. x² = 1, 2, 3 …). At a jump the product is discontinuous unless the other factor is zero there; even then the left and right derivatives differ because the floor value changes by 1, so the point is still a corner. Count all jump points in the interval.
Algebra: Functions||floor × polynomial d.w: Dropping the point where the other factor vanishes (it is continuous, but not differentiable), or missing a jump at the end of the interval.

Algebra: Functions||kinks of min/max of.m: min(sin x, cos x) or max(…) changes branch exactly where the two functions are equal; solve sin x = cos x (or the given equation) in the interval. Each crossing at which the slopes differ is a non-differentiable point.
Algebra: Functions||kinks of min/max of.w: Counting tangential touches (equal slopes) as kinks, or missing crossings near the ends of the interval.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: A linear expression over a polygon is largest and smallest at the vertices. Find each vertex by solving pairs of boundary lines, check it satisfies the remaining constraints, then evaluate the expression there. If the inequalities are strict the range is an open interval.
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Using a non-feasible intersection point, or writing a closed interval when the inequalities are strict.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: If the roots are in ratio m : n, write them as mk and nk. Then sum = (m + n)k and product = mn·k²; eliminate k to get a condition on the coefficients: (sum)²·mn = (product)(m + n)².
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Forgetting that k can be negative, or mixing up which root takes which ratio – the relation is symmetric, so it does not matter, but the arithmetic must be consistent.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log and d.m: Convert the log equation to exponential form, or use change of base so that all logs share one base. For log_a b · log_b a type relations, remember log_a b = 1/log_b a.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log and d.w: Ignoring the domain: arguments must be positive and bases positive and ≠ 1. Reject solutions outside the domain.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log of a.m: log_{ab} x = log x ÷ (log a + log b). Use this to express everything in the logs of the prime factors, then solve the resulting linear relation.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log of a.w: Writing log_{ab} x = log_a x + log_b x. It is not additive in the base.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||nested mo.m: Work from the inside out: split at the zero of the inner modulus, solve each region separately, then re-check every solution against the region it came from.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||nested mo.w: Solving without regions and then accepting extraneous roots that fall outside the region.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||sum of ab.m: The graph of |x − a| + |x − b| + … is piecewise linear with breakpoints at a, b, …; its minimum is at the median breakpoint. Evaluate at the breakpoints and compare.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||sum of ab.w: Taking the mean of the breakpoints rather than the median.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||AP with sum.m: Express every term as a + (k − 1)d, form two equations from the given sum and product (or ratio), and solve for a and d. Check with the requested term.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||AP with sum.w: Assuming a particular term is the middle one without verifying the number of terms is odd.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||AP × GP inf.m: For Σ (a + nd) rⁿ, multiply by r and subtract: S(1 − r) = a + d·r/(1 − r), so S = a/(1 − r) + d·r/(1 − r)². Valid only for |r| < 1.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||AP × GP inf.w: Using the pure GP sum formula, or applying the formula when |r| ≥ 1 and the series diverges.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||k·k! telesc.m: k·k! = (k + 1)! − k!, so Σ k·k! from 1 to n = (n + 1)! − 1. Telescoping cancels everything except the ends.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||k·k! telesc.w: Trying to compute each term; look for the difference-of-two-terms form first.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||ratio of su.m: If S_n : S′_n = (An + B) : (Cn + D), then the ratio of the m-th terms is obtained by putting n = 2m − 1 (the middle-term trick), since S_n = n × (middle term) for odd n.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||ratio of su.w: Substituting n = m directly. The m-th term corresponds to 2m − 1 terms in the sum, not m.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||telescoping.m: Split each term by partial fractions into a difference f(k) − f(k + 1); then almost all terms cancel and only the first and last survive.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||telescoping.w: Cancelling the wrong pairs – write out the first three and last three terms to see exactly what survives.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||telescoping.m: Rationalise 1/(√k + √(k+1)) = √(k+1) − √k. The sum then collapses to √(n+1) − √1.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||telescoping.w: Forgetting to rationalise. The terms look unrelated until you multiply by the conjugate.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||telescoping.m: For terms like 1/(k(k + m)) use 1/m · (1/k − 1/(k + m)). The surviving terms are the first m and last m reciprocals, not just one on each end.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||telescoping.w: Treating a shift of m like a shift of 1 and cancelling only the neighbours.

Algebra: Sets & Relations||counting rela.m: A relation on n elements is a subset of the n² ordered pairs. Reflexive forces the n diagonal pairs; symmetric means pairs come in mirrored couples (n(n − 1)/2 free choices off the diagonal). Count free binary choices and take powers of 2.
Algebra: Sets & Relations||counting rela.w: Counting ordered pairs when the relation is symmetric – each mirrored pair is a single choice, not two.

Algebra: Sets & Relations||set identitie.m: Reduce with De Morgan and distributive laws, or test with a Venn diagram/element-membership table. Check each of the eight regions for the final expression.
Algebra: Sets & Relations||set identitie.w: Assuming A − B = B − A or that complement distributes over union without flipping it to an intersection.

Averages||group change over time.m: When members leave or join, track the total (average × count), not the average. New total = old total − leavers' ages + joiners' ages (after adjusting for the passage of time: +years × members).
Averages||group change over time.w: Forgetting that everyone ages together. Remaining members each add the same number of years.

Averages||partial means.m: Convert each given mean to a total (mean × count); then subtract or add totals to isolate the group of interest, and divide by its own size.
Averages||partial means.w: Averaging the averages without weighting by group sizes.

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||growt.m: Convert each growth rate to a multiplier (1 + g/100) and multiply along the chain. Intermediate values are needed for comparisons between years.
DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||growt.w: Adding percentages. Successive changes compound, and a +25% followed by −20% leaves you exactly where you began.

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||pie +.m: Convert the pie percentage to an absolute count using the stated total, then apply the bar's percentage to that count (male %, female = 100 − male %). Combine groups in absolute numbers before taking ratios.
DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||pie +.w: Averaging the two percentages for combined groups; the cities have different sizes.

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||two p.m: Each pie must be converted using its own total. Compare absolute values, not shares, when the totals differ.
DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||two p.w: Reading a rise in share as a rise in value. If the total changed, the share can rise while the value falls.

DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||l.m: Join the two tables on the shared label, compute the derived column (units sold × price, or good units × price), then answer. Write intermediate values in a small table.
DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||l.w: Using units produced instead of units sold, or ignoring a defect/return rate given in the other table.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||cone fr.m: The small cone cut off is similar to the whole cone: lengths scale by k, areas by k², volumes by k³. Frustum = whole − small cone.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||cone fr.w: Scaling volumes by k or k² rather than k³; or forgetting to subtract the cut-off cone.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||inradiu.m: For any triangle r = Area ÷ s (s = semi-perimeter). For a right triangle r = (a + b − c)/2. Quote the area ratio with the circle's area πr².
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||inradiu.w: Using the circumradius formula (c/2) or the wrong semi-perimeter.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||interse.m: When two chords meet inside a circle, the products of the segments are equal: PX·XQ = RX·XS.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||interse.w: Multiplying whole chords instead of the two segments of each.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||recasti.m: Melting and recasting preserves volume: equate total volumes, cancel π, and divide. Note whether wastage or hollow parts are mentioned.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||recasti.w: Equating surface areas instead of volumes.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||tangent.m: Tangents from one external point are equal in length. In a right triangle with an incircle, the tangents from the right-angle vertex both equal r.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||tangent.w: Mixing up the tangent length from a vertex with the radius for non-right triangles.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||tangent.m: PT² = PA·PB where PA is the near and PB the far intersection. The chord AB = PB − PA.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||tangent.w: Using PA·AB, or equating PT with PB.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||two sec.m: PA·PB = PC·PD with each product taken from the same external point to the near and far points. Subtract to get the chord length.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||two sec.w: Using a chord length where the full secant (external + chord) belongs.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||cevians.m: Assign masses so that each cevian's foot balances its side; the ratio in which the cevians cut each other follows from the masses. Then convert length ratios to area ratios using shared heights.
Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||cevians.w: Placing masses on the wrong ends (the larger mass goes on the shorter segment).

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||polygon.m: Interior angle sum = 180(n − 2); each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360/n. Set up one equation from the stated relation and solve.
Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||polygon.w: Using n instead of (n − 2), or mixing interior and exterior angles.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||polygon.m: Diagonals = n(n − 3)/2. Solve the given relation for n; reject non-integer or non-positive roots.
Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||polygon.w: Using n(n − 1)/2, which also counts the sides.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||trapeziu.m: The diagonals divide the trapezium into four triangles. The two triangles on the parallel sides are similar with area ratio (a : b)²; the two side triangles have equal area = √(product of those two).
Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||trapeziu.w: Taking the area ratio as a : b instead of a² : b².

Geometry: Trigonometry||height & distanc.m: Draw the figure and write tan(angle) = height ÷ horizontal distance for each observation. Equate the unknown horizontal distances, then solve.
Geometry: Trigonometry||height & distanc.w: Using sin or cos by mistake, or measuring the angle of depression from the vertical.

Geometry: Trigonometry||trig identities.m: From sin θ + cos θ = s, square to get sin θ cos θ = (s² − 1)/2. Then express the target using sin²+cos² = 1, a³+b³ = (a+b)(a² − ab + b²) and tan+cot = 1/(sin cos).
Geometry: Trigonometry||trig identities.w: Dropping the factor of 2 when squaring, or using sin⁴+cos⁴ = 1 − sin²cos² instead of 1 − 2 sin²cos².

Higher Math: Definite Integration||King'.m: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx. Add the two forms of I; the integrand often simplifies to a constant, giving 2I = (b − a) × constant.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||King'.w: Forgetting to adjust the limits or to divide by 2 at the end.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||area.m: Find intersection points first, then integrate (upper − lower) between them. Split where the curves cross.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||area.w: Integrating (lower − upper) and getting a negative answer, or using the wrong limits.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||defin.m: Apply ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du, evaluate uv at the limits, then integrate the remaining term. Choose u by ILATE.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||defin.w: Forgetting to evaluate the boundary term uv between the limits.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||integ.m: Find where the expression inside |·| changes sign, split the integral there, and integrate the positive version on each part.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||integ.w: Integrating f(x) over the whole interval and then taking the modulus of the result.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||odd/e.m: Over [−a, a], odd functions integrate to 0 and even functions to twice the integral over [0, a]. Split the integrand into odd and even parts first.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||odd/e.w: Using the shortcut when the interval is not symmetric about 0.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||perio.m: If f has period T, ∫ over any interval of length nT = n × ∫ over one period. Reduce the limits using this before integrating.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||perio.w: Using the number of periods incorrectly when the interval is not a whole multiple of T.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: Express the cone's volume in a single variable using the geometry of the sphere (r² = R² − (h − R)²), differentiate, set to zero, and confirm it is a maximum.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Skipping the check that the stationary point is a maximum, or leaving two variables.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: Factorise f′ and sign-test across each root: a change from + to − is a local maximum, − to + a local minimum, no change is neither. Repeated roots (even power) do not change sign.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Treating every root of f′ as an extremum, even where f′ does not change sign.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: Minimise the square of the distance D² = (x − a)² + (f(x) − b)² (it has the same minimiser and avoids square roots). Differentiate, solve, and check it is a minimum.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Minimising D instead of D² without care, or taking a point that is not on the curve.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: Relate the variables with similar triangles (r/h fixed), write V in terms of one variable, then differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Differentiating before eliminating the second variable, or treating r and h as independent.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: The slope of the tangent at x = c is f′(c); the line is y − f(c) = f′(c)(x − c). Substitute the given condition (point or intercept) and solve.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Using the slope formula at the wrong point, or forgetting to compute f(c) for the point of contact.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||com.m: Write ax² + bx + c = a[(x + h)² + k²], then use ∫ dx/(u² + k²) = (1/k) tan⁻¹(u/k). Do not forget the 1/a outside.
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||com.w: Dropping the leading coefficient a, or the 1/k factor.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||e^x.m: Since d/dx [eˣ f(x)] = eˣ(f + f′), any integrand of this form integrates to eˣ f(x). Differentiate the proposed answer and match coefficients.
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||e^x.w: Matching only the highest power; the lower coefficients carry through the derivative term.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||ini.m: Integrate, then use the given condition to fix the constant. For f(b) − f(a) = ∫ₐᵇ f′, you can skip the constant altogether.
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||ini.w: Forgetting the constant of integration, or using the wrong sign for ∫ from a to b when b < a.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||par.m: Factorise the denominator, write the sum of A/(x − a) + B/(x − b), and find A, B by the cover-up rule. Integrate each term to get logarithms.
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||par.w: Forgetting that ∫ 1/(x − a) dx = ln|x − a| (modulus), or sign errors when covering up.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||rep.m: Integrate f″ to get f′ + constant, use the stationary-point condition for the constant, integrate again, then use the value condition.
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||rep.w: Using the value condition on f′ or the stationary condition on f.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||sub.m: Substitute u for the inner expression and rewrite x in terms of u. Expand and integrate each power separately.
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||sub.w: Forgetting to convert x as well as dx; leaving a mix of x and u.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||tri.m: Write the numerator as A·(denominator) + B·(derivative of denominator). Then the integral is A·x + B·ln|denominator|.
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||tri.w: Sign errors in the derivative of the denominator (derivative of sin x + cos x is cos x − sin x).

Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.m: Continuity: left limit = right limit = value. Differentiability: in addition left and right derivatives match. Set up equations in the parameters at each join point.
Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.w: Using only continuity when differentiability is demanded; the derivative must match too.

Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.m: Replace each function with its series (sin x ≈ x − x³/6, eˣ ≈ 1 + x + x²/2, ln(1 + x) ≈ x − x²/2) up to the order that survives the cancellation, then divide.
Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.w: Truncating too early, so that the leading terms cancel and nothing is left.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.m: The determinant with rows (1, aᵢ, aᵢ²) equals the product of (aⱼ − aᵢ) for i < j. For a GP, substitute aᵢ = a·rⁱ and simplify.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.w: Reversing the order of subtraction, which flips the sign.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.m: For an n×n matrix, det(adj A) = (det A)^{n−1}, det(kA) = kⁿ det A, and det(AB) = det A · det B. Compose these rather than computing matrices.
Compute A², A³ to see the pattern; for [[x, 1],[0, 1]] the (1,2) entry is a geometric sum (xⁿ − 1)/(x − 1). Prove by induction if needed.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.w: Assuming Aⁿ simply raises each entry to the n-th power.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.m: Use the characteristic equation to write A² in terms of A and I, then reduce higher powers step by step. Aⁿ = pA + qI with p, q found recursively.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.w: Computing high powers directly. Reduce with the characteristic polynomial.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.m: Compute the determinant of the coefficient matrix as a function of the parameter. Unique solution when it is non-zero; if zero, compare ranks to decide between no solution and infinite solutions.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.w: Declaring "no solution" whenever the determinant is zero – check consistency first.

Mixtures & Alligations||two-vessel trans.m: After each transfer, track the quantity of each ingredient in both vessels. Use (1 − x/V)ⁿ for repeated removal and replacement from one vessel.
Mixtures & Alligations||two-vessel trans.w: Treating the second vessel as pure after mixing, or forgetting that the removed amount carries the current proportion.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Count arrangements using n!/(p! q! …) for repeated letters; handle conditions (vowels together, specific letters apart) by gluing or the gap method.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Forgetting to divide by the factorial of repeated letters, or double counting when letters are glued.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: For x₁ + … + xₖ = n with upper bounds, count without bounds by stars and bars C(n + k − 1, k − 1), then subtract cases where a variable exceeds its bound (inclusion–exclusion).
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Subtracting only one violating case when two variables can violate simultaneously.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Fix one person to break symmetry: n people around a circle gives (n − 1)!. For "together", treat the group as one object and multiply by its internal arrangements.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Using n! for a circle, or forgetting that reflections count separately unless the arrangement is a necklace.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Split into cases by the constraint (a particular person included/excluded, at least k of a type) and add; or use total minus the forbidden cases.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Double counting committees that satisfy two cases at once.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: The number of shortest paths in an a × b grid is C(a + b, a). With forced or forbidden points, multiply the path counts of the two segments or subtract paths through the forbidden point.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Counting through a forced point as a sum rather than a product.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Fix the last digit(s) by the divisibility test (even, multiple of 5, digit sum multiple of 3 …), then count the remaining positions, taking care over the leading zero.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Letting the first digit be 0, or double counting when digit repeats are allowed.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Choose which items are in the right place, then derange the rest using D₂ = 1, D₃ = 2, D₄ = 9, D₅ = 44.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Using n! for the rest. A derangement has no fixed point.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Count words that start with each smaller letter in turn (using n!/repeats), then move to the next position. Add 1 for the word itself.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Forgetting to adjust for repeated letters or to add 1 at the end.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Group identical letters. Count selections by cases on how many of each repeated letter are chosen, or use a product of (1 + r) factors for the possible numbers.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Treating identical letters as different when only selecting (not arranging).

Modern Math: Set Theory||overlap bounds.m: Minimum overlap of three sets inside a universe: max(0, a + b + c − 2n). Maximum overlap is the size of the smallest set. Check with a Venn diagram.
Modern Math: Set Theory||overlap bounds.w: Applying the two-set formula to three sets.

Modern Math: Set Theory||three-set Venn.m: Fill the central region first, then the pairwise-only regions (pair total − centre), then the single-only regions, and finally the "none" region.
Modern Math: Set Theory||three-set Venn.w: Subtracting the pair total instead of pair-only regions, which double subtracts the centre.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.m: Combined variance = weighted mean of variances + weighted variance of the means: σ² = (n₁σ₁² + n₂σ₂²)/(n₁ + n₂) + n₁n₂(μ₁ − μ₂)²/(n₁ + n₂)².
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.w: Averaging the two variances and ignoring the gap between the means.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.m: List the outcomes satisfying the condition (the reduced sample space) and count how many of those satisfy the event. P(A|B) = n(A ∩ B)/n(B).
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.w: Dividing by 36 rather than by the size of the conditional space.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.m: Use Bayes' theorem: P(source | event) = P(source)P(event | source) ÷ Σ P(source)P(event | source).
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.w: Using the prior instead of the posterior, or forgetting to include every source in the denominator.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||e.m: Add up the cases of exactly k successes: for k = 1, P(A)(1 − P(B))(1 − P(C)) + … Each case multiplies the relevant probabilities.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||e.w: Using the binomial formula when the probabilities differ between events.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||e.m: E[X] = Σ x·P(x). For games with a repeated structure, set up an equation for E from the first step.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||e.w: Using the probabilities that do not sum to 1 or forgetting costs/payoffs.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||t.m: Let p be the probability the first player wins; condition on the first throw and use the repeating structure to get p = P(win now) + P(both fail)·p. Solve for p.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||t.w: Summing only the first few rounds, or mixing up who throws first.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||u.m: Track the urn composition after each draw. For Pólya's urn, the probability of a given colour at the second draw equals that at the first; use symmetry or the law of total probability.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||u.w: Assuming draws are independent. The urn changes after each draw.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||v.m: σ² = Σ f·x²/N − (Σ f·x/N)². Compute both sums once and subtract; don't recompute deviations for each class.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||v.w: Using N − 1 in the denominator for a population, or forgetting to square the mean.

Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.m: Reduce each term mod 100 using the cycle of powers (or Euler: 20-cycle for odd bases coprime to 100), add, and take mod 100.
Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.w: Using the cycle for the last digit (mod 10) when the last two digits are asked.

Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.m: Factor the base into primes. Trailing zeros of n! in base b = min over primes p^e of ⌊(exponent of p in n!)/e⌋.
Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.w: Counting only factors of the larger prime or ignoring the exponent e.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||H.m: Write the numbers as H·a and H·b with a, b coprime. Then product = H × LCM, and LCM = H·a·b. Enumerate coprime pairs for the required product.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||H.w: Allowing pairs that are not coprime, which gives a larger HCF.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||c.m: Prime factorise; the number of divisors is Π(eᵢ + 1). Odd divisors ignore the factor 2; square divisors take even exponents only.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||c.w: Counting divisors including 1 and the number when the question excludes them (or vice versa).

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||s.m: If N leaves remainder r_i on division by d_i with a constant gap (d_i − r_i = k), then N = LCM(d_i)·m − k. Otherwise solve pairwise congruences.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||s.w: Using the LCM with the remainder added instead of the gap subtracted.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||el.m: Total votes = valid + invalid. Winner's margin comes from valid votes only; set up an equation in terms of valid votes.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||el.w: Applying the percentages to total votes when they refer to valid votes.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||ma.m: Take cost per unit as 100. A customer pays for fewer units than they receive, so revenue comes from the paid units only: paid × 100(1 + x/100)(1 − d) must equal total cost of all units given × (1 + target profit). Solve for x.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||ma.w: Treating the free item as a plain discount, or taking the profit on revenue instead of on the cost of every unit given out.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||ov.m: Compute the cost of each article from its selling price and gain/loss %, then compare total SP with total CP. If the SP is equal and gain% = loss%, there is always a net loss.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||ov.w: Averaging the profit percentages. They apply to different cost bases.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||pr.m: Revenue = price × quantity. A price rise of p% and a volume fall of q% gives a multiplier (1 + p/100)(1 − q/100). Invert to find the required change.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||pr.w: Adding the percentages instead of multiplying the multipliers.

Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||recipro.m: Convert to a form like x/y + y/x = k, put t = x/y and solve t + 1/t = k for t. Then back-substitute into the ratio asked.
Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||recipro.w: Taking only one root of the quadratic; both t and 1/t give the same ratio swapped.

Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||sequent.m: Work backwards from the final state, undoing each transfer, or keep a table of the amounts after each step. Use unitary values for the unknown start.
Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||sequent.w: Applying the transfers in the wrong order or to the wrong person.

Simple & Compound Interest||equal instal.m: Equate the present value of the instalments to the loan: P = x/(1 + r) + x/(1 + r)² + …. Solve for x; for CI use the GP sum.
Simple & Compound Interest||equal instal.w: Adding the interest to each instalment separately without discounting.

Simple & Compound Interest||growth every.m: Rate per period r with n periods per year: amount = P(1 + r)ⁿᵗ. Match the rate to the compounding period, then apply the multiplier.
Simple & Compound Interest||growth every.w: Using the annual rate with the number of half-years.

Simple & Compound Interest||split invest.m: Let the parts be x and (total − x). Set up an equation using total interest or equality of amounts, and solve the linear equation.
Simple & Compound Interest||split invest.w: Mixing up the principal of each part or using the wrong time period.

Time & Work||efficiency with unknown day.m: Let the unknown days be d and use efficiency = 1/d for each worker. Write one equation from the combined work and solve the quadratic if it appears.
Time & Work||efficiency with unknown day.w: Using days instead of efficiency in the sum.

Time & Work||one worker leaves.m: Work done before leaving + work done after = 1. Use each worker's efficiency over the time they actually worked.
Time & Work||one worker leaves.w: Assuming the leaver worked for the full time.

Time & Work||pipes in rotation.m: Compute the net work (or water) per full cycle, find how many complete cycles occur, then handle the remainder carefully within the next cycle.
Time & Work||pipes in rotation.w: Counting the remainder at the wrong point in the cycle or ignoring that the task finishes mid-cycle.

Time, Speed & Distance||all runners meet.m: For meeting anywhere on the track, each pair meets every (lap length ÷ relative speed); the three are together at the LCM of those intervals. For meeting at the start, use the LCM of individual lap times instead.
Time, Speed & Distance||all runners meet.w: Using the LCM of the speeds, or mixing up 'together at the start' with 'together anywhere'.

Time, Speed & Distance||boat and changin.m: Use upstream = b − s, downstream = b + s. Set up separate time equations for each leg, and solve the simultaneous equations for the unknown speed.
Time, Speed & Distance||boat and changin.w: Using the boat speed for the whole journey or the same stream speed on both legs when it changes.

Time, Speed & Distance||three runners at.m: Convert each speed to laps per unit time and take the LCM of the time per lap to find when they are all at the start together.
Time, Speed & Distance||three runners at.w: Treating "meet anywhere" and "at the start" as the same thing.

Time, Speed & Distance||train passes a p.m: The train covers its own length relative to the passenger: time = length ÷ relative speed. For a platform, add the platform length.
Time, Speed & Distance||train passes a p.w: Adding speeds when the objects move the same way, or ignoring the length of the platform.

LR: Syllogisms||three statements, three.m: Draw a Venn diagram for the statements, accepting them as true. Start with the universal statements, then add the particular ones. A conclusion is correct only if it holds in every possible diagram.
LR: Syllogisms||three statements, three.w: Accepting a conclusion that is merely possible. 'Definitely follows' means it must be true in all diagrams.

LR: Syllogisms||two statements, two conc.m: Convert to A/E/I/O forms. Valid inferences: All A are B + All B are C ⇒ All A are C; No A are B ⇒ No B are A; Some A are B ⇒ Some B are A. Check each conclusion against these, and check the complementary pair (either/or) rule.
LR: Syllogisms||two statements, two conc.w: Concluding 'All' from two 'Some' statements, or from 'No' + 'All' without the proper conversion.

LR: Linear & Circular Seating||circular.m: Fix one person, place others by clockwise/anticlockwise and 'between' clues. In a circle, left and right swap when someone faces outward; note whether they face the centre. Use the direct clues first.
LR: Linear & Circular Seating||circular.w: Fixing a seat arbitrarily without noting direction (clockwise vs anticlockwise).

LR: Linear & Circular Seating||row arran.m: Draw the row with numbered slots. Place the fixed-position clues first (ends, middle), then relative clues (next to, between). Use elimination to settle the rest.
LR: Linear & Circular Seating||row arran.w: Assuming left means the same side for everyone. Check which way they face.

LR: Scheduling & Days||weekly schedule.m: Make a grid of people × days. Put definite clues first, then use 'before/after' to narrow ranges. Eliminate days already taken.
LR: Scheduling & Days||weekly schedule.w: Applying 'immediately after' as 'after'. It means the very next day.

LR: Ranking & Ordering||ranking.m: Total people = rank from top + rank from bottom − 1. Place people on a number line using 'above/below' clues and fill the gaps with the remaining names.
LR: Ranking & Ordering||ranking.w: Counting the person twice, or forgetting the −1.

LR: Blood Relations||plain chain.m: Convert each statement to a single relation and chain them step by step, drawing a small family tree with gender symbols.
LR: Blood Relations||plain chain.w: Assuming gender from names. Use only what is given.

LR: Blood Relations||coded relations.m: Decode each symbol first (A $ B means B is the brother of A), write each statement as a relation, then chain them from left to right.
LR: Blood Relations||coded relations.w: Reading the relation from the wrong side. In 'B is the brother of A', B is the brother.

LR: Blood Relations||reverse relation.m: In 'the person is the son of my mother's only son', work from the speaker: speaker → mother → her son (the speaker's brother or the speaker himself) → his son.
LR: Blood Relations||reverse relation.w: Forgetting that the mother's only son could be the speaker himself.

LR: Direction Sense||distance.m: Set coordinates: start at (0, 0), north = +y, east = +x. Update after each move, then use Pythagoras for the straight-line distance.
LR: Direction Sense||distance.w: Adding all the lengths instead of using the net displacement.

LR: Direction Sense||turns.m: Right turn = clockwise, left = anticlockwise. Convert turns to quarter-turns (90° each) and add them up modulo 360°.
LR: Direction Sense||turns.w: Mixing up clockwise with anticlockwise when combining turns.

LR: Direction Sense||direction.m: Track the final position relative to the start with a quick sketch; the direction is where the end point lies from the start.
LR: Direction Sense||direction.w: Giving the direction of the last move rather than the final position from the start.

LR: Direction Sense||relative position.m: Place the speaker first, mark the facing direction, then place the others using left/right relative to the speaker's facing.
LR: Direction Sense||relative position.w: Using the object's left as the observer's left.

LR: Coding-Decoding||letter shift.m: Compare letter by letter using alphabet positions (H→J is +2). Apply the same shift to the new word, wrapping after Z.
LR: Coding-Decoding||letter shift.w: Spotting the pattern from one letter only. Check all letters.

LR: Coding-Decoding||alternating shift.m: Different positions may have different shifts (+2, −3, +2, −3 …). Find the shift for each position and apply it to the new word.

LR: Coding-Decoding||word transformation.m: Check for two steps: reversal followed by a shift (or the reverse). Test each step on the example before applying it to the new word.

LR: Coding-Decoding||sum.m: Convert each letter to its alphabet position (A = 1 … Z = 26) and add. Use the pairs summing to 27 (A–Z, B–Y) to check quickly.

LR: Coding-Decoding||phrase decoding.m: Compare phrases that share a word to find that word's code, then eliminate known codes to decode the rest.
LR: Coding-Decoding||phrase decoding.w: Matching codes by position instead of by shared words.

LR: Coding-Decoding||pos_weighted.m: Multiply each letter's value by its position in the word (1st letter × 1, 2nd × 2, …) and add.
LR: Coding-Decoding||pos_weighted.w: Using the alphabet position as the weight.

LR: Coding-Decoding||sum_vowels.m: Pick out only the vowels (A, E, I, O, U) in the word, take their alphabet values, and add.
LR: Coding-Decoding||sum_vowels.w: Including consonants, or counting Y as a vowel.

LR: Number & Letter Series||fibo.m: Each term is the sum of the previous two (or a similar combination). Test a₃ = a₁ + a₂ on the given numbers.

LR: Number & Letter Series||wrong term.m: Find the pattern from most terms, then locate the one that breaks it. Check differences, ratios or squares and cubes.
LR: Number & Letter Series||wrong term.w: Assuming the first or last term is wrong without testing.

LR: Number & Letter Series||letter-numbe.m: Treat the letters and numbers as separate series: letters advance by +1 and numbers by +1. Combine them.
LR: Number & Letter Series||letter-numbe.w: Treating the pair as a single pattern.

LR: Number & Letter Series||letter serie.m: Convert letters to numbers (A = 1 …) and find the pattern in the numbers. Convert back, wrapping at Z.

LR: Number & Letter Series||diffap.m: The differences between terms themselves form an AP (e.g. +2, +4, +6). Extend the difference series and add.
LR: Number & Letter Series||diffap.w: Looking at ratios when the differences already show the pattern.

LR: Number & Letter Series||alt.m: Two interleaved series: take every other term and check each sub-series separately.
LR: Number & Letter Series||alt.w: Searching for a single rule through all terms.

LR: Number & Letter Series||ap.m: A constant difference between terms. Add the common difference to the last term.
LR: Number & Letter Series||ap.w: Using the wrong difference by checking only one pair.

LR: Number & Letter Series||cubepm.m: Terms are cubes ± a constant (n³ + 2 etc.). Compare each term with nearby cubes.
LR: Number & Letter Series||cubepm.w: Overlooking a cube because the offset is small.

LR: Number & Letter Series||gp.m: A constant ratio between terms. Multiply the previous term by the common ratio.
LR: Number & Letter Series||gp.w: Adding the difference instead of multiplying.

LR: Number & Letter Series||primes.m: The terms are consecutive primes. List primes in order to find the missing one.
LR: Number & Letter Series||primes.w: Missing a prime between the given terms.

LR: Number & Letter Series||mixed_ap.m: The differences themselves follow a pattern (such as +9, +11, +13). Extend it one step.
LR: Number & Letter Series||mixed_ap.w: Treating it as a plain AP.

LR: Number & Letter Series||sqpm.m: Terms are squares ± a constant (n² + 2 …). Compare each term with nearby squares.

LR: Number & Letter Series||mulplus.m: Pattern ×2 + k (or ×3 − k …) between successive terms. Solve the rule from the first two terms and test on the next.
LR: Number & Letter Series||mulplus.w: Testing the rule on only one pair.

LR: Number & Letter Series||diff2.m: Squares of consecutive integers (4 = 2², 9 = 3² …). The next term is the next square.
LR: Number & Letter Series||diff2.w: Picking the next number by the difference only.

LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||odd one.m: Convert letters to positions and check relationships: gaps, reversals or sums. The odd group breaks the shared rule.
LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||odd one.w: Choosing a group because it looks different instead of testing the rule.

LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||letter-s.m: Find how the letters in the first group move to make the second (reverse, swap, shift). Apply the same movement to the missing group.
LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||letter-s.w: Using only the first triad to infer the rule.

LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||letter a.m: Identify the operation that turns the first word into the second (here reversal), then apply it to the third.
LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||letter a.w: Treating it as a shift when it is a rearrangement.

LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||vowel_be.m: Mark each vowel, look at the next letter, and count the vowel–consonant pairs.
LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||vowel_be.w: Counting the vowels that are followed by another vowel or by nothing.

LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||letters_.m: Letters between X and Y = |pos(X) − pos(Y)| − 1.
LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||letters_.w: Forgetting to subtract 1 (the letters themselves are not counted).

LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||same_pos.m: Compare each letter's position from the start with its position from the end of the alphabet (position + reverse position = 27).
LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns||same_pos.w: Reversing the word instead of the alphabet.

LR: Number Operations||operation chain.m: Find the single operation (multiply, add, square) that maps the first number to the second in the first example. Verify it on the others and apply it.
LR: Number Operations||operation chain.w: Fixing on a rule that works for one example only.

LR: Number Operations||pair rule.m: Find a rule f(a, b) that fits the given pairs (e.g. a·b − k or a² − b²). Test it on all examples, then compute the new pair.
LR: Number Operations||pair rule.w: Settling on a rule after checking one example.

LR: Data Sufficiency||circular seating s.m: Draw the circle and place people using the first statement only; see whether the answer is fixed. Repeat with the second, then both.
LR: Data Sufficiency||circular seating s.w: Using information from statement II while testing statement I alone.

LR: Data Sufficiency||quantitative suffi.m: Treat each statement as an equation. Count unknowns versus independent equations; check whether the question can be answered uniquely from I, II, or both.
LR: Data Sufficiency||quantitative suffi.w: Calling a statement sufficient when it gives a range, not one value.

LR: Statement-Action & Cause||reasons fo.m: Pick the options that directly explain the event described, not just ones that are related. Eliminate options that are unrelated or that contradict the statement.
LR: Statement-Action & Cause||reasons fo.w: Choosing an option that is true but does not explain the statement.

LR: Statement-Action & Cause||courses of.m: A good course of action is practical, addresses the problem, and has no harmful side-effects. Judge each course on those grounds, not on whether it sounds good.

LR: Statement-Action & Cause||assumption.m: An assumption is something taken for granted that the statement needs to be sensible. Test: if the assumption were false, would the statement fall apart?
LR: Statement-Action & Cause||assumption.w: Selecting a fact that is merely true or merely related.

VARC: Vocabulary - Synonyms||synonym in.m: Read the sentence, decide whether the word is positive, negative or neutral, then pick the option closest in meaning and tone.
VARC: Vocabulary - Synonyms||synonym in.w: Picking a word that is related but not interchangeable.

VARC: Vocabulary - Antonyms||antonym.m: First work out the meaning of the word, then find the option with the opposite meaning. Beware of options that are synonyms of the word.
VARC: Vocabulary - Antonyms||antonym.w: Picking a synonym by mistake when the question asks for the opposite.

VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||fil.m: Read the whole sentence for the clue (contrast words like 'but', cause words like 'because'). Predict the meaning before looking at the options.
VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context||fil.w: Choosing a word that fits grammatically but not logically.

VARC: Vocabulary - Meanings & Definition.m: Eliminate words whose meaning you know to be different, and look at the word's root or tone for the remaining options.
VARC: Vocabulary - Meanings & Definition.w: Choosing a word that sounds similar to the definition.

VARC: Vocabulary - Meanings & Definition.m: Think of the word in a sentence you have seen it in; use roots and prefixes as clues (trans- = across).
VARC: Vocabulary - Meanings & Definition.w: Guessing from the sound of the word.

VARC: Idioms & Phrases||meaning of an id.m: Idioms are fixed expressions and their meanings are not literal. Learn the idiom as a whole; eliminate literal readings.

VARC: Idioms & Phrases||idiom from meani.m: Match the meaning to the idiom by imagining the situation it describes; eliminate those with clearly different meanings.
VARC: Idioms & Phrases||idiom from meani.w: Picking an idiom with similar words rather than similar meaning.

VARC: One-word Substitution||one word fo.m: Look for the key idea in the phrase (e.g. eats everything → omnivorous) and match the root of the word with the idea.
VARC: One-word Substitution||one word fo.w: Picking a word that sounds similar but means something else.

VARC: One-word Substitution||phrase for.m: Break the word into its root and suffix to work out its meaning, then match with the phrase.
VARC: One-word Substitution||phrase for.w: Choosing a phrase that is merely related.

VARC: Verbal Analogies||analogy.m: First state the relationship in a sentence (pen is used to write; knife is used to cut). Then find the option that fits the same sentence.
VARC: Verbal Analogies||analogy.w: Choosing a word that is related to 'knife' but doesn't fit the relationship.

VARC: Grammar - Subject-Verb Agreement||.m: Find the true subject (ignoring phrases in between) and match the verb to it in number. Watch for 'each', 'either', 'neither', which are singular.
VARC: Grammar - Subject-Verb Agreement||.w: Matching the verb to the nearest noun.

VARC: Grammar - Subject-Verb Agreement||.m: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb unless they form a single idea. 'Either…or' follows the nearer subject.
VARC: Grammar - Subject-Verb Agreement||.w: Treating a single idea (bread and butter) as plural.

VARC: Grammar - Prepositions & Collocati.m: Many verbs and adjectives take a particular preposition (suffering from, interested in, good at). Learn them as pairs.
VARC: Grammar - Prepositions & Collocati.w: Using a preposition that sounds right in Hindi or Tamil but not in English.

VARC: Grammar - Tenses & Verb Forms||ten.m: Look for time markers (since, for, yesterday, by the time). Match tense to the time relationship in the sentence.
VARC: Grammar - Tenses & Verb Forms||ten.w: Using simple past with 'since' instead of present perfect.

VARC: Grammar - Articles, Pronouns & Det.m: Use 'a/an' for a non-specific singular noun and 'the' for a specific one. After a preposition use the object pronoun (between you and me).
VARC: Grammar - Articles, Pronouns & Det.w: Using the subject pronoun after a preposition.

VARC: Grammar - Error Spotting||error sp.m: Read each part and test: subject-verb agreement, tense, preposition, pronoun case. Choose 'No error' only if all parts pass.
VARC: Grammar - Error Spotting||error sp.w: Marking the part that sounds odd rather than the part that breaks a rule.

VARC: Grammar - Commonly Confused Words|.m: Learn the pairs by meaning (lie/lay, affect/effect). Substitute each into the blank and test the sentence meaning.

VARC: Para Jumbles - Sentence Ordering||.m: Find the opening sentence (introduces the topic, has no pronoun pointing back). Then link sentences with connectors, pronouns and time order.
VARC: Para Jumbles - Sentence Ordering||.w: Starting with a sentence that refers to something not yet mentioned.

VARC: Para Jumbles - Odd Sentence & Open.m: The opening introduces the topic; the closing concludes or gives a consequence. Look for words like 'therefore', 'thus', 'consequently' in the last sentence.
VARC: Para Jumbles - Odd Sentence & Open.w: Choosing a sentence that mentions the topic but depends on an earlier sentence.

VARC: Para Jumbles - Odd Sentence & Open.m: Find the main topic from the majority of sentences; the odd one speaks about a different subject, even if it sounds related.
VARC: Para Jumbles - Odd Sentence & Open.w: Rejecting a sentence just because it is harder to understand.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - tone.m: Look at the author's choice of adjectives and verbs. Match the overall attitude (critical, neutral, appreciative) to the option, avoiding extremes unless the text is strong.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - tone.w: Choosing an extreme tone for a mildly worded passage.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - detail.m: Go back to the passage and find the line that supports the answer. The correct option paraphrases it; wrong options distort or exaggerate it.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - detail.w: Choosing an option that is true in general but not stated in the passage.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - main i.m: The main idea covers the whole passage, not just one paragraph. Wrong options are too narrow, too broad, or off-topic.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - main i.w: Picking a detail from the second paragraph as the main idea.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - infere.m: An inference follows logically from what is stated, with no outside knowledge. Test: could the author disagree? If so, it is not an inference.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - infere.w: Choosing an option that goes beyond the text.

VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - applic.m: Identify the author's position, then pick the option most consistent with it, applied to a new case.
VARC: Reading Comprehension||RC - applic.w: Choosing an option that is consistent with common sense but not with the author.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||ma.m: Work backwards from the target: required SP = CP × (1 + profit%). Then SP = MP × (1 − discount%), so MP = SP ÷ (1 − d). Profit is on cost; discount is on marked price.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||ma.w: Applying the discount to cost price, or the profit to marked price. Two different bases are in play.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||pr.m: Expenditure = price × consumption. If price rises by p%, new consumption must be old × 1/(1 + p/100) to keep expenditure fixed. Reduction % = p/(100 + p) × 100.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||pr.w: Answering 'same percentage' (e.g. 100% rise → 100% cut). The base changes: a 100% price rise needs only a 50% cut in use.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||su.m: Convert each change to a multiplier (+10% → 1.10, −30% → 0.70) and multiply. Net change = product − 1. Order does not matter for the final value.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||su.w: Adding or subtracting the percentages. Each change applies to the new value, not the original.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||pa.m: Set the pass mark as a single unknown. 'Fails by 10' → pass = score + 10; 'gets 20 more than pass' → pass = score − 20. Equate the two expressions, solve for the total, then the pass mark.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||pa.w: Mixing up 'fails by' (below pass) and 'passes by' (above pass), which flips the sign of the gap.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||eq.m: When two items sell at the same SP with gain g% on one and loss g% on the other, the net result is always a loss of (g/10)²%. In general compute each CP = SP ÷ (1 ± r) and compare totals.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||eq.w: Assuming gain and loss cancel. The loss item cost more, so the loss is bigger in rupees than the gain.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||eq.m: Two discounts a% and b% equal one discount of a + b − ab/100 %. Or multiply the retention factors: (1 − a/100)(1 − b/100), then subtract from 1.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||eq.w: Adding the discounts (50 + 15 = 65). The second discount applies to an already reduced price.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||fa.m: The dealer gives only the false weight but charges for the true weight, so gain from the weight alone = (true − false)/false × 100. If he also marks up and discounts, multiply the factors: overall SP/CP = (1 + markup)(1 − discount) × (true/false).
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||fa.w: Using the true weight as the denominator. The goods actually handed over are the false weight, so that is the base.

Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||su.m: Marked price = CP × (1 + markup). Apply each discount in turn: MP × (1 − d1) × (1 − d2). Profit% = (SP − CP)/CP × 100.
Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount||su.w: Treating a markup and a discount of the same percent as cancelling: +50% then −10% is not +40%.

Simple & Compound Interest||CI-SI differ.m: For 2 years, CI − SI = P(r/100)². For 3 years, CI − SI = P(r/100)²(3 + r/100). Use these directly instead of computing both interests.
Simple & Compound Interest||CI-SI differ.w: Using the 2-year formula for 3 years. The third year also earns interest on interest from year 2.

Simple & Compound Interest||compound int.m: A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ and CI = A − P. For small whole rates use successive multiplication (×1.05 three times) rather than powers.
Simple & Compound Interest||compound int.w: Reporting the amount A as the interest. CI is A minus principal.

Simple & Compound Interest||SI growth.m: SI = P·r·t/100. If the sum becomes k times itself, interest = (k − 1)P, so r·t = 100(k − 1). Divide by t to get r.
Simple & Compound Interest||SI growth.w: Using k·P as the interest. A sum that triples earned only 2P of interest.

Simple & Compound Interest||rate from am.m: At compound interest, consecutive amounts have a constant ratio: A₃/A₂ = 1 + r/100. Divide the later amount by the earlier one, subtract 1.
Simple & Compound Interest||rate from am.w: Subtracting the amounts and dividing by principal, which is the simple-interest method.

Simple & Compound Interest||half-yearly.m: Halve the rate and double the periods: r/2 per half-year for 2n periods. 1.5 years at 20% p.a. = 3 half-years at 10%. Multiply 1.1 three times for A.
Simple & Compound Interest||half-yearly.w: Keeping the annual rate with doubled periods. The rate per period must be halved too.

Simple & Compound Interest||SI to CI.m: Find P from SI: P = SI × 100/(r·t). Then compute CI = P[(1 + r/100)ⁿ − 1] for the stated n.
Simple & Compound Interest||SI to CI.w: Assuming CI equals SI because the rate and time match. They only agree in year 1.

Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||partner.m: Profit shares are in the ratio of (capital × time). Compute each product, reduce, then split the profit in that ratio.
Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||partner.w: Using capital alone when the investments ran for different durations.

Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||income-.m: Let incomes be a·x, b·x and expenses c·y, d·y. Equal savings gives two equations in x and y. Solve for x/y, then substitute back.
Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||income-.w: Treating the ratios as actual amounts. Ratio units differ for income and expenditure.

Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||combine.m: Link A:B and B:C by making the common term equal (scale each ratio so B matches), then write A:B:C. Share = total × part/sum.
Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||combine.w: Joining ratios without matching the middle term, e.g. writing 2:3 and 4:5 as 2:3:5.

Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||ratio c.m: Write the numbers as ax and bx. After the change, set up (ax + k)/(bx + k) = new ratio and cross-multiply to find x.
Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||ratio c.w: Adding the amount to only one term, or to the ratio parts instead of the actual numbers.

Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||ratio s.m: Replace x = 7k and y = 5k (the common factor cancels). Substitute into the expression and simplify; the k disappears.
Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||ratio s.w: Substituting 7 and 5 into only one of the numerator and denominator.

Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||late jo.m: Convert each investment to capital × months, using each partner's own period in the business. Split profit in that ratio.
Ratio, Proportion & Partnership||late jo.w: Counting the full year for the partner who joined late.

Averages||replacement.m: Change in total = (new − old) = change in average × number of members. So new person = old person + n × (change in average).
Averages||replacement.w: Dividing by the wrong n, or forgetting that the total changes by the difference, not the new value alone.

Averages||wrong reading.m: Correct total = wrong total − wrong value + right value. Divide by n for the correct mean.
Averages||wrong reading.w: Correcting the average directly without first working with totals.

Averages||average speed.m: When equal distances are covered at speeds a and b, average speed = 2ab/(a + b) (harmonic mean), not the arithmetic mean. For equal times it is (a + b)/2.
Averages||average speed.w: Taking the simple mean of the speeds when distances are equal.

Averages||weighted average.m: Average = (n₁a₁ + n₂a₂)/(n₁ + n₂). With the final average known, use alligation: the gaps to the mean are in inverse ratio of the group sizes.
Averages||weighted average.w: Averaging the two averages without weighting by group size.

Averages||batting average.m: Total runs so far = innings × average. New average = (total + new score)/(innings + 1). Solve for the unknown score or average.
Averages||batting average.w: Forgetting to add 1 to the number of innings in the denominator.

Averages||AP average.m: In an arithmetic progression the average is (first + last)/2. For the first n odd numbers it is n.
Averages||AP average.w: Computing the full sum first. The shortcut avoids long arithmetic.

Averages||member leaves.m: Total before = n × old average; total after = (n − 1) × new average. The leaver's age = total before − total after.
Averages||member leaves.w: Using n instead of n − 1 for the new group size.

Mixtures & Alligations||alligation (pric.m: Alligation: cheaper : dearer = (dearer − mean) : (mean − cheaper). Draw the cross and read off the ratio of quantities.
Mixtures & Alligations||alligation (pric.w: Putting the ratio the wrong way round. The quantity of the cheaper is proportional to the gap on the dearer side.

Mixtures & Alligations||replacement.m: After replacing x from volume V (repeated n times), pure part left = V(1 − x/V)ⁿ. For a single replacement subtract once.
Mixtures & Alligations||replacement.w: Reducing by the same amount each time. Each removal takes out a diluted mixture.

Mixtures & Alligations||dilution.m: Amount of acid stays constant. Acid = concentration × volume; new volume = acid ÷ new concentration; water added = new volume − old volume.
Mixtures & Alligations||dilution.w: Adding the percentage points instead of tracking the amount of pure substance.

Mixtures & Alligations||mixing solutions.m: Add the pure amounts and the volumes separately: concentration = (c₁V₁ + c₂V₂)/(V₁ + V₂).
Mixtures & Alligations||mixing solutions.w: Averaging the two percentages without weighting by volume.

Mixtures & Alligations||three alloys.m: With a fixed ratio of the three alloys, take the weighted average of the three percentages using the ratio parts as weights.
Mixtures & Alligations||three alloys.w: Using the percentages as weights instead of the ratio of quantities.

Mixtures & Alligations||add water ratio.m: Split the mixture by the original ratio, add the extra water, and set up the new ratio equation. Solve for the unknown quantity.
Mixtures & Alligations||add water ratio.w: Adding the water to both parts or changing the milk quantity.

Time, Speed & Distance||trains crossing.m: Crossing time = sum of lengths ÷ relative speed (opposite direction: add speeds; same direction: subtract). Convert km/h to m/s by × 5/18.
Time, Speed & Distance||trains crossing.w: Forgetting to convert units, or using only one train's length.

Time, Speed & Distance||boats and stream.m: Downstream = boat + stream; upstream = boat − stream. Time = distance ÷ the relevant speed. For a round trip add both times.
Time, Speed & Distance||boats and stream.w: Using still-water speed for both directions.

Time, Speed & Distance||late/early.m: Let the distance be d. Write d/s₁ − d/s₂ = time difference and solve for d. Times are inversely proportional to speeds at fixed distance.
Time, Speed & Distance||late/early.w: Treating the time difference as the travel time itself.

Time, Speed & Distance||meeting point.m: Starting towards each other: meeting time = distance ÷ (sum of speeds). Distance from either end = that speed × time.
Time, Speed & Distance||meeting point.w: Using the difference in speeds when they move towards each other.

Time, Speed & Distance||circular track.m: First meeting in the opposite direction occurs after track length ÷ (sum of speeds); in the same direction, track length ÷ (difference). When they meet again at the start, use LCM of their lap times.
Time, Speed & Distance||circular track.w: Mixing the opposite- and same-direction formulas.

Time, Speed & Distance||train and platfo.m: The pole gives the train's speed: speed = length ÷ time. Crossing a platform means covering train length + platform length at that speed.
Time, Speed & Distance||train and platfo.w: Dividing only the platform length by speed.

Time, Speed & Distance||time saved.m: Compute the new time at the faster speed (distance ÷ speed), subtract from the old time, and convert hours to minutes at the end.
Time, Speed & Distance||time saved.w: Leaving the answer in hours when minutes are asked.

Time & Work||combined work.m: Add rates: 1/a + 1/b is the work done per day together. Time together = 1 ÷ (1/a + 1/b) = ab/(a + b).
Time & Work||combined work.w: Adding the days (18 + 36) instead of the rates.

Time & Work||leaving early.m: Work done before someone leaves = days × combined rate. The remaining fraction is finished at the remaining person's rate. Total time = days together + remaining ÷ rate.
Time & Work||leaving early.w: Assuming the total time equals the time of the person who leaves.

Time & Work||pipes and cisterns.m: Inlets are positive rates, leaks negative. Net rate = Σ(1/t). Time to fill = 1 ÷ net rate. If the net rate is negative, the tank empties.

Time & Work||efficiency ratio.m: If A is k times as efficient as B, A takes 1/k of B's time. Combined rate = (k + 1) units for B's unit rate. Solve using the days together.
Time & Work||efficiency ratio.w: Taking 'twice as efficient' to mean twice the time.

Time & Work||man-days.m: Work = men × days × hours (× efficiency). Equate the work in both scenarios, then solve for the unknown quantity.
Time & Work||man-days.w: Ignoring hours per day when it changes between scenarios.

Time & Work||wages.m: Wages are shared in proportion to work done (rate × days worked). Compute each person's fraction of work, then split the total pay.
Time & Work||wages.w: Splitting equally because all worked the same number of days, when their rates differ.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||H.m: For two numbers, product = HCF × LCM. Find the unknown number = (HCF × LCM) ÷ the known one.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||H.w: Applying this to three numbers. The identity holds only for two.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||L.m: Numbers leaving the same remainder r when divided by several divisors have the form LCM·k + r. Take k = 0 for the smallest.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||L.w: Forgetting to add the remainder after finding the LCM.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||H.m: To find the greatest divisor leaving the same remainder, take HCF of the pairwise differences of the numbers.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||H.w: Taking the HCF of the numbers themselves.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||L.m: Events recurring every a, b, c minutes coincide every LCM(a, b, c) minutes. Convert to clock time by adding the LCM to the start time.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||L.w: Using the HCF, or forgetting to convert minutes into hours.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||i.m: Exactly one of A or B = n(A) + n(B) − 2n(A ∩ B). Counts: multiples of m up to N = ⌊N/m⌋. Both: multiples of LCM.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||i.w: Using n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B), which counts 'at least one'.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||d.m: A number is divisible by 9 if its digit sum is a multiple of 9; by 3 likewise with 3; by 11 if the alternating digit sum is a multiple of 11. Solve for the missing digit.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||d.w: Choosing a digit that gives a sum divisible by 3 only when 9 is required.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||d.m: If N = p^a·q^b·r^c, number of divisors = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1). Odd divisors come from the odd primes only.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||d.w: Counting 1 and N incorrectly, or including the factor 2 when asked for odd divisors.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||t.m: Largest square tile = HCF of the length and breadth. Number of tiles = (L × B) ÷ tile area.
Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility||t.w: Using LCM, which gives the smallest square that tiles with no cutting.

Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.m: Units digits cycle with period 1, 2 or 4. Reduce the exponent modulo the cycle (use 4 when the remainder is 0) and read the digit from the cycle.
Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.w: Using exponent 0 instead of the last position of the cycle when the remainder is 0.

Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.m: Find the cycle of remainders of the base modulo the divisor, or reduce the base first (11 ≡ 2 mod 9). Then reduce the exponent modulo the cycle length.
Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.w: Reducing the exponent modulo the divisor instead of the cycle length.

Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.m: Largest power of a prime p in n! = ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + … For a composite base, do this for each prime and take the minimum after dividing by its exponent.
Trailing zeros = min(power of 2, power of 5) in the prime factorisation. Break each base into primes and add the exponents.
Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.w: Counting only factors of 10 that appear explicitly.

Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.m: From k! onward, k! is a multiple of the modulus once all its prime powers appear. Sum only the earlier terms and reduce.
Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.w: Computing the whole sum, which is unnecessary.

Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.m: Last two digits = number mod 100. Use the cycle of powers mod 100 (cycles often have length 20 or 4). Reduce the exponent and compute.
Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.w: Using the unit-digit cycle for two-digit questions.
