Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: Sum of roots = −b/a; product = c/a. Express the quantity: α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ; α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β).
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Solving for the roots explicitly, which is slower and error-prone with surds.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: f(a) is the remainder on dividing by (x − a). Write f(x) = quotient × (x − a)(x − b) + (px + q); use the two remainders to solve for p and q.
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Assuming the remainder is a constant when dividing by a quadratic.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: Equal roots need b² − 4ac = 0. Real distinct roots need > 0; no real roots need < 0. Solve the resulting equation for the unknown.
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Setting b² = 4ac with a sign slip on the constant term.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: Use the sum and product of roots: x² − (sum)x + product = 0. Compare coefficients to find p and q.
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Forgetting the minus sign on the sum in the standard form.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: Look for a combination that gives the requested expression directly (add or subtract the equations) instead of solving for both variables.
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Solving fully and making arithmetic errors when a direct combination existed.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: Square or cube the given: (x + 1/x)² = x² + 1/x² + 2; (x + 1/x)³ = x³ + 1/x³ + 3(x + 1/x).
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Forgetting the cross-term 3(x + 1/x) in the cube.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: Let roots be kα and α. Use sum = −b/a and product = c/a to get two equations in α and k, then solve for the constant.
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Assuming integer roots when only the ratio is given.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: Solve each inequality separately, intersect the intervals, and count the integers inside, watching strict versus non-strict signs.
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Including an endpoint when the inequality is strict.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.m: Let the younger age be x and write both 'now' and 'later' ages as equations. Substitute and solve the linear system.
Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.w: Applying the future ratio to current ages.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||AP terms.m: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. Subtract two given terms to get d = (Tₘ − Tₙ)/(m − n); then back-substitute for a.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||AP terms.w: Off-by-one: the nth term uses (n − 1), not n.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||S(n) to T(n.m: Tₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ (for n ≥ 2). Substitute n and n − 1 into the formula and subtract.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||infinite GP.m: Sum to infinity = a/(1 − r) with |r| < 1. Solve for r = 1 − a/S.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||infinite GP.w: Using the finite sum formula, or an r outside (−1, 1).

Algebra: Sequences & Series||AP × GP.m: Express the terms of A and B as formulas in n, set the equality, and solve the resulting equation. Test small values of n when needed.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||AP × GP.w: Matching terms at different indices instead of the same index.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||series sums.m: Telescoping: 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n − 1/(n+1), so the sum collapses to 1 − 1/(N+1). Also remember Σn = N(N+1)/2 and Σn² = N(N+1)(2N+1)/6.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||series sums.w: Adding the first few terms by hand and guessing the pattern.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||AM-GM-HM.m: For two positive numbers, AM × HM = GM². So GM = √(AM × HM). Then recover the numbers from AM and GM.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||recurrence.m: Compute term by term using the rule (a₂ = 2a₁ + 1, …). For long recurrences look for a closed form.
Algebra: Sequences & Series||recurrence.w: Applying the rule to the wrong previous term.

Algebra: Sequences & Series||finite GP.m: Tₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹. Find r by dividing consecutive terms, then raise to the (n − 1)th power.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||point-line.m: Distance of (x₁, y₁) from ax + by + c = 0 is |ax₁ + by₁ + c|/√(a² + b²).
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||point-line.w: Dropping the absolute value, which can give a negative distance.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||line tange.m: A line is tangent to a circle when its perpendicular distance from the centre equals the radius. Put the line in general form and solve for c.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||line tange.w: Equating the line with the circle's equation and forgetting that tangency means exactly one solution.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||triangle a.m: Area = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||triangle a.w: Leaving out the ½ or the absolute value.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||parallel/p.m: Parallel lines have equal slopes (a₁/b₁ = a₂/b₂); perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1 (a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = 0).

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||intercepts.m: Set y = 0 for the x-intercept and x = 0 for the y-intercept. Area of the triangle with the axes = ½ × |x-int| × |y-int|.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||intercepts.w: Using the equation coefficients directly as intercepts without dividing.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||circle.m: Complete the square: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c). Then use the distance formula.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||circle.w: Reading the centre as (g, f) with the wrong sign.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||collineari.m: Three points are collinear if the area of the triangle is zero, or if the slopes between pairs are equal. Set up an equation in the unknown.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||collineari.w: Equating the wrong pairs of slopes.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||centroid.m: Centroid = average of the three vertices: ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3). Solve for the missing vertex.
Algebra: Coordinate Geometry||centroid.w: Using the midpoint formula, which divides by 2.

Algebra: Sets & Relations||counting rela.m: A relation from A to B is any subset of A × B. If |A × B| = m, there are 2^m relations.
Algebra: Sets & Relations||counting rela.w: Counting only functions or only the non-empty ones.

Algebra: Sets & Relations||relation prop.m: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for all a. Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R. Transitive: (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R. Test each with a small example.
Algebra: Sets & Relations||relation prop.w: Calling '≤' symmetric because equal pairs are symmetric. One counterexample (1, 2) breaks symmetry.

Algebra: Sets & Relations||two-set Venn.m: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). Total = n(A ∪ B) + neither. Rearrange to find the overlap.
Algebra: Sets & Relations||two-set Venn.w: Forgetting to add the 'neither' group to the total.

Algebra: Sets & Relations||set operation.m: List the elements explicitly, apply the operation, then count. A − B means in A but not in B; complements are taken inside U.
Algebra: Sets & Relations||set operation.w: Taking the complement of the wrong set, or counting elements of B in A − B.

Algebra: Sets & Relations||equivalence c.m: a R b if a − b is divisible by m splits the numbers into m residue classes. Count of classes = m (if the range is large enough).
Algebra: Sets & Relations||equivalence c.w: Counting each element as its own class.

Algebra: Functions||domain.m: The domain is every x where the expression is defined: denominators ≠ 0, square-root arguments ≥ 0, log arguments > 0. Solve the resulting inequality.
Algebra: Functions||domain.w: Using ≥ 0 for a logarithm argument. It must be strictly positive.

Algebra: Functions||functional equation.m: Substitute x and 1/x to get two equations in f(x) and f(1/x). Solve the pair simultaneously, then plug in the required x.
Algebra: Functions||functional equation.w: Substituting only once. A single equation has two unknowns.

Algebra: Functions||composition.m: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)): work from the inside out. Evaluate the inner function first.
Algebra: Functions||composition.w: Applying the functions in the wrong order.

Algebra: Functions||inverse function.m: Set y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y, and swap. For a value, solve f(x) = given value directly instead.

Algebra: Functions||quadratic extrema.m: Check the vertex x = −b/2a. If it lies in the interval, compare f at the vertex and both endpoints; otherwise compare the endpoints.
Algebra: Functions||quadratic extrema.w: Reporting the vertex value when the vertex lies outside the interval.

Algebra: Functions||counting functions.m: One-one functions from m to n elements (m ≤ n): nPm = n!/(n − m)!. All functions: nᵐ. Onto functions need inclusion-exclusion.

Algebra: Functions||even/odd functions.m: Even: f(−x) = f(x); odd: f(−x) = −f(x). Substitute −x into each candidate and simplify.
Algebra: Functions||even/odd functions.w: Assuming every polynomial with even powers is even without checking constants and cross-terms.

Algebra: Functions||greatest integer fun.m: ⌊x⌋ jumps at every integer. Count the integers strictly inside the interval; endpoints are excluded when the interval is open.
Algebra: Functions||greatest integer fun.w: Counting endpoints that lie outside the open interval.

Algebra: Functions||bijections.m: A function is bijective if it is both one-one (strictly monotonic) and onto (range = codomain). Check each option's behaviour on ℝ.
Algebra: Functions||bijections.w: Choosing x² or |x|, which are not one-one on ℝ.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||sum of mo.m: Split the number line at the critical points (where each modulus is zero) and solve the linear equation in each region. Reject solutions outside their region.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||sum of mo.w: Accepting a solution that doesn't lie in the region where its sign assumption holds.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||modulus i.m: |f(x)| < a means −a < f(x) < a. Solve the double inequality and count the integers.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||modulus i.w: Writing only one side of the inequality.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log equat.m: Combine logs into one: log(ab) = log a + log b. Convert to exponent form, solve the quadratic, then discard roots that make any original argument ≤ 0.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log equat.w: Forgetting the domain check. A root may be extraneous.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log evalu.m: Reduce each log to an integer using log_b(bⁿ) = n. Keep signs carefully when logs are subtracted.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log evalu.w: Dropping the negative sign in front of the first term.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||number of.m: Digits of N = ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ + 1. Here log₁₀(7³⁰) = 30 × 0.8451; take the integer part and add 1.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||number of.w: Forgetting the +1, or rounding instead of flooring.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||logs in t.m: Break the number into prime factors, e.g. 80 = 2⁴ × 5, and use log 5 = 1 − log 2 (since 2 × 5 = 10). Substitute p.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||logs in t.w: Using log 5 = log 10 − log 2 without noticing log 10 = 1.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log prope.m: Change of base: log_{aᵏ}(x) = (1/k) log_a x; log_a(xᵐ) = m log_a x. Combine the exponents and use the given value.
Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms||log prope.w: Pulling a power out of the base as k instead of 1/k.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||Heron's.m: s = (a + b + c)/2; area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)); inradius r = area ÷ s.
Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||Heron's.w: Dividing the area by the perimeter instead of s.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||polygons.m: Diagonals of an n-gon = n(n − 3)/2. Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°; each exterior angle of a regular polygon = 360°/n.
Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||polygons.w: Using nC2 without subtracting the n sides.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||similar.m: DE ∥ BC gives AD/AB = DE/BC = AE/AC. Remember AB = AD + DB, and use the full side on the denominator.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||right tr.m: Pythagoras: a² + b² = c². Learn the triples (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25) and multiples.
Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||right tr.w: Squaring wrongly when the unknown is a leg rather than the hypotenuse.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||angles i.m: The circumcentre is equidistant from the vertices. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so ∠BOC = 2∠A, and triangle OBC is isosceles.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||equilate.m: In an equilateral triangle the centroid, incentre and circumcentre coincide; R = 2r, so r : R = 1 : 2.
Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||equilate.w: Confusing the ratio with the median or altitude lengths.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||angle bi.m: The bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides: BD/DC = AB/AC. Then use BD + DC = BC.
Geometry: Triangles & Polygons||angle bi.w: Using BD/DC = AC/AB, which is the wrong way round.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||paralle.m: Distance from the centre to a chord = √(r² − (c/2)²). For chords on opposite sides, add the two distances; on the same side, subtract.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||paralle.w: Always adding the distances without checking which side each chord lies.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||cone fr.m: When a sector is rolled into a cone, the sector radius becomes the slant height, and the sector's arc length becomes the base circumference. Solve for r and then h.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||cone fr.w: Using the sector radius as the cone's radius.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||recasti.m: Volume is conserved: n × (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)πR³, so R = r × ∛n. Surface area then changes by a different factor.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||tangent.m: Length of a direct common tangent = √(d² − (r₁ − r₂)²); transverse = √(d² − (r₁ + r₂)²). Pick the one that matches the question.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||tangent.w: Using the sum of radii for a direct tangent.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||arc and.w: Mixing the area and arc formulas.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||cuboids.m: Volume = lwh; total surface area = 2(lw + wh + hl); diagonal = √(l² + w² + h²).
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||cuboids.w: Using the surface-area formula for volume.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||circle.m: Tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment. The angle at the centre is twice that at the circumference on the same arc.
Geometry: Circles & Mensuration||circle.w: Taking the tangent-chord angle as the central angle.

Geometry: Trigonometry||sin A + cos A.m: Square the given: (sin A + cos A)² = 1 + 2 sin A cos A. Solve for sin A cos A.
Geometry: Trigonometry||sin A + cos A.w: Forgetting that sin²A + cos²A = 1 inside the expansion.

Geometry: Trigonometry||heights and dist.m: Draw the figure and write tan(angle) = height ÷ horizontal distance for each point. Use two such equations to eliminate the unknown distance.
Geometry: Trigonometry||heights and dist.w: Using sin or cos where the data gives horizontal distance.

Geometry: Trigonometry||standard values.m: Memorise: sin 30° = ½, cos 60° = ½, tan 45° = 1, sec 45° = √2, sin 60° = √3/2. Substitute and simplify.
Geometry: Trigonometry||standard values.w: Reading sec as cos. sec² 45° = 2, not ½.

Geometry: Trigonometry||ratios from tan.m: Draw a right triangle with opposite = 8 and adjacent = 15, hypotenuse = √(8² + 15²) = 17. Read off the other ratios.
Geometry: Trigonometry||ratios from tan.w: Using the wrong side as the hypotenuse.

Geometry: Trigonometry||extreme values.m: For a sin θ + b cos θ, the maximum is √(a² + b²) and the minimum is −√(a² + b²).
Geometry: Trigonometry||extreme values.w: Adding a and b instead of using the square root.

Geometry: Trigonometry||complementary an.m: tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, so pair the angles: tan 35° · tan 55° = 1 and tan 40° · tan 50° = 1.

Geometry: Trigonometry||addition formula.m: sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B. Find the missing cosines from sin² + cos² = 1 (positive for acute angles).

Modern Math: Set Theory||three-set Venn.m: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = ΣA − Σ(pairs) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C). Fill the Venn from the centre outwards: triple overlap, then pairs only, then singles.
Modern Math: Set Theory||three-set Venn.w: Subtracting the pair overlaps without adding back the triple overlap.

Modern Math: Set Theory||counting subset.m: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, 2ⁿ − 1 non-empty, 2ⁿ − 2 non-empty proper subsets.

Modern Math: Set Theory||overlap bounds.m: Minimum overlap = max(0, sum − 100%); maximum overlap = the smaller set.
Modern Math: Set Theory||overlap bounds.w: Reporting the maximum when the minimum is asked.

Modern Math: Set Theory||multiples sets.m: Count multiples with ⌊N/k⌋. For intersections use the LCM. Then apply union/difference formulas.
Modern Math: Set Theory||multiples sets.w: Using the product instead of the LCM when the numbers share factors.

Modern Math: Set Theory||power set of pr.m: n(A × B) = n(A)·n(B) = m; the number of relations is 2^m, and non-empty relations are 2^m − 1.
Modern Math: Set Theory||power set of pr.w: Forgetting to subtract the empty relation.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Treat the vowels as a block, arrange the block with the other letters, then arrange inside the block. Divide by factorials for repeated letters.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Forgetting to divide by the repeated letters in both stages.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: 'At least' cases: add the separate cases (exactly 2 women, exactly 3 women) or use total minus the unwanted case. Use nCr for each.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Using one nCr for a combined case and double counting.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Arrange the unrestricted items first; the restricted items go into the gaps (n + 1 gaps for n items), chosen with nCr, then arranged.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Counting adjacent arrangements when separation is required.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: n distinct objects around a circle: (n − 1)!; necklaces (flippable): (n − 1)!/2.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Using n! or forgetting the division by 2 for necklaces.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: With repetition allowed, each position has the same number of choices: nᵏ for k positions. Watch for a leading-zero restriction.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Using permutation formulas when repetition is allowed.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Distributing n identical items into k boxes: C(n + k − 1, k − 1). With a minimum per box, subtract the minimum first.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Forgetting to subtract the minimum before applying the formula.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Group by pattern: all alike, two alike + one different, all different. Count each pattern and add.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Missing a pattern, or treating identical letters as different.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Lines = nC2; diagonals = nC2 − n; triangles = nC3. Subtract collinear sets when points lie on a line.
List the pairs that make the sum (5,6) and (6,5) for 11. For distinguishable dice order counts.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Counting each unordered pair once for distinguishable dice.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.m: Count words starting with each earlier letter (k! each), then move to the next position. Rank = words before + 1.
Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.w: Forgetting the +1 for the word itself.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.m: P(A|B) = n(A ∩ B)/n(B) in equally likely outcomes. Restrict the sample space to B first.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.w: Using the full sample space as the denominator.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||r.m: Bayes: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Draw a two-way table with the given figures and read the cell you need.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||d.m: Without replacement, multiply successive probabilities with decreasing totals, or use combinations: C(good, k)/C(total, k).
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||d.w: Keeping the denominator constant after a ball is removed.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||i.m: For independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). 'At least one' = 1 − P(none) = 1 − Π(1 − pᵢ).

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.m: A deck has 52 cards: 4 suits × 13, 12 face cards, 4 aces. Use C(favourable, 2)/C(52, 2) for two cards without replacement.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.w: Forgetting to remove the first card for the second draw.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||l.m: For y = ax + b: mean(y) = a·mean(x) + b; SD(y) = |a|·SD(x). Adding a constant does not change spread.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||l.w: Multiplying the SD by a and also adding b.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||w.m: Compute the mean μ = Σpᵢxᵢ, then variance = Σpᵢxᵢ² − μ². Use the weights given.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||e.m: E(X) = Σ x·P(x), counting losses as negative. Compute each outcome's value times its probability and sum.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||b.m: For n tosses of a fair coin, P(k heads) = C(n, k)/2ⁿ. Add the relevant terms for 'at most' or 'at least'.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||b.w: Computing only the single term for k.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.m: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). For n fair tosses: 1 − 1/2ⁿ.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||c.w: Calculating several cases by hand when the complement is one term.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||m.m: Sort the data first. Median is the middle value (or the average of the two middle values if n is even); mode is the most frequent.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||m.w: Taking the middle of the unsorted list.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||v.m: Mean μ = Σx/n; population variance = Σ(x − μ)²/n (or Σx²/n − μ²). Divide by n, not n − 1, for a population.
Modern Math: Statistics & Probability||v.w: Dividing by n − 1 when the data is the whole population.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.m: For a 3×3 matrix expand along a row with zeros: Σ ±aᵢⱼ Mᵢⱼ with signs +−+ along the first row. For 2×2: ad − bc.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.w: Missing the alternating sign in the cofactor expansion.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.m: For 2×2 [a b; c d], inverse = (1/(ad − bc)) [d −b; −c a]. Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.w: Forgetting to divide by the determinant or flipping the wrong signs.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.m: |AB| = |A||B|. Find each determinant separately instead of multiplying the matrices.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.w: Multiplying the matrices first and making errors.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.m: Write the determinant as an expression in k (ad − bc) and set it equal to the given value. Solve the linear equation.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.w: Reversing the products in the 2×2 determinant.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.m: Minor Mᵢⱼ is the determinant after deleting row i and column j; cofactor Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i + j) Mᵢⱼ.
A 2×2 symmetric matrix has 3 free entries (a, b, c) so with k choices each: k³ matrices. A general n×n symmetric has n(n + 1)/2 free entries.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.m: Use Cramer's rule or elimination. Cramer: x = Dₓ/D, with D the determinant of the coefficients, provided D ≠ 0.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.w: Using Dₓ with the wrong column replaced.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.m: If D = 0: the system has infinitely many solutions when the equations are proportional (including the constants), no solution otherwise.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.w: Declaring 'no solution' without checking whether the constants are proportional too.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.m: If A² = A (idempotent), then Aⁿ = A for all n ≥ 1. Expand (I + A)ⁿ by the binomial theorem; all A-power terms collapse to A.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.w: Forgetting that I and A commute here so the binomial theorem applies.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.m: adj(A) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. The (i, j) entry of adj(A) is the cofactor Cⱼᵢ (note the swap).
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.w: Reading the (i, j) cofactor without transposing.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.m: Look for patterns: triangular matrices (product of the diagonal), Vandermonde (product of differences), or zero rows/columns.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.w: Expanding blindly when a structure gives the answer quickly.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.m: Solve by elimination one variable at a time, using the equation with the most zeros first. Substitute back to find all three before multiplying.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.w: Multiplying partial values before solving fully.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.m: Three points are collinear iff the determinant |x₁ y₁ 1; x₂ y₂ 1; x₃ y₃ 1| = 0. Expand and solve for the unknown.
Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.w: Putting the points in the matrix without the column of ones.

Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.m: If direct substitution gives 0/0, factorise numerator and denominator, cancel the common factor, and substitute again.
Divide the numerator and denominator by the highest power of x. The limit is the ratio of leading coefficients when the degrees are equal.
Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.w: Ignoring lower-degree terms incorrectly when the degrees differ.

Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.m: Use lim sin x/x = 1, lim (eˣ − 1)/x = 1, lim ln(1 + x)/x = 1, all as x → 0. Match the argument inside and outside.
Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.w: Having a different argument inside and outside (e.g. ln(1 + 5x)/x gives 5, not 1).

Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.m: For f continuous at a, left limit = right limit = f(a). Equate the two pieces at the junction and solve for the constant.
Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.w: Evaluating both pieces on the same side.

Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.m: Check the left and right derivatives at the suspect point. Functions with corners (like |x|) fail; x|x| is smooth at 0.
For 0/0 use series or L'Hôpital: differentiate numerator and denominator separately, then substitute again.
Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.w: Using the quotient rule instead of differentiating top and bottom separately.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: Differentiate term by term (d/dx xⁿ = n xⁿ⁻¹), then substitute the point.
Chain rule: d/dx [f(g(x))] = f′(g(x))·g′(x). Don't forget the inner derivative.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Forgetting the derivative of the inner function.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: Set f′(x) = 0 for the critical point, test with f″(x) (positive → minimum), and evaluate f at that point.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Reporting the x-value when the value of f is asked.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: Slope of the tangent = f′(a); line: y − f(a) = f′(a)(x − a). Set x = 0 for the y-intercept.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Using the point's coordinates in the wrong order.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: Write the quantity as a function of one variable using the constraint, differentiate, set to zero, and check it is a maximum or minimum.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Forgetting the domain restriction on the variable.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: f increases where f′ > 0. Stationary points are the roots of f′ = 0; for a quadratic f′, the sum of roots is −b/a.
For implicit curves differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function: x² + y² = r² ⇒ 2x + 2y y′ = 0 ⇒ y′ = −x/y.
Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.w: Forgetting y′ when differentiating y terms.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.m: Write the geometric relationship, differentiate with respect to time, then substitute the instantaneous values. For the ladder: x² + y² = L² ⇒ x ẋ + y ẏ = 0.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||ant.m: Integrate term by term (∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)), use F(0) = 0 to fix the constant, then evaluate.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||sub.m: Let u = the inner expression, du = its derivative dx. For ∫ x e^{2x²} dx let u = 2x², du = 4x dx.
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||sub.w: Forgetting to adjust for the missing constant factor in du.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||ant.m: For a definite integral use the antiderivative F and compute F(b) − F(a).
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||ant.w: Treating a definite integral as an indefinite one.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||int.m: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Choose u as the part that simplifies on differentiating (x), dv as the part easy to integrate (eᵃˣ).
Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||int.w: Choosing u and dv the wrong way round.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration||sta.m: ∫ sec²(ax) dx = tan(ax)/a; ∫ eᵃˣ dx = eᵃˣ/a; ∫ cos(ax) dx = sin(ax)/a. Divide by the coefficient of x.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||polyn.m: Antiderivative first, then F(upper) − F(lower). Keep signs carefully with negative limits.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||polyn.w: Sign errors with a negative lower limit.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||prope.m: ∫ₐᶜ = ∫ₐᵇ + ∫ᵦᶜ for any b. Reversing the limits flips the sign.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||prope.w: Adding integrals that don't share an endpoint.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||area.m: Area = ∫ f(x) dx between the limits when f ≥ 0. Where f is negative, take its absolute value over that piece.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||area.w: Treating negative parts as positive area without splitting.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||stand.m: ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x|. So ∫₁ᵏ 1/x dx = ln k. Solve ln k = ln 4.

Higher Math: Definite Integration||subst.m: With u = sin x, the limits change from x to u values, so you never convert back. ∫ sin x cos x dx = ½ sin² x.
Higher Math: Definite Integration||subst.w: Keeping the x-limits after substituting u.

DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||t.m: Share = part ÷ total × 100; growth % = (new − old)/old × 100. Identify the base before calculating.
DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||t.w: Using the new value as the base.

DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||t.m: Read the right rows and columns carefully, then do one subtraction or ratio. Note the unit stated in the table header.
Use the row or column total relationship to find the missing value: missing = total − sum of known values.
DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||t.w: Choosing the wrong row for the total.

DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||u.m: km/h → m/s: multiply by 5/18; m/s → km/h: multiply by 18/5. Always attach units through the calculation.

DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||t.m: Combine the tables: value = price × quantity for each row. Compute the two totals, then take the difference or ratio.
DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||t.w: Using the same row of the wrong table.

DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||t.m: Sum the relevant cells first, then compute the ratio or percentage on the sum, not on individual cells.

DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||D.m: A change in percentage points is the simple difference between the percentages (60% → 35% is a 25-point fall), not a percentage change of the percentage.
DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions||D.w: Reporting the percentage change (about 41.7%) when points are asked.

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||bar g.m: Read the exact bar heights for the required categories, then add or compare. Check the axis units.
DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||bar g.w: Misreading the scale or picking the wrong series.

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||line.m: Compute growth % for each consecutive pair: (later − earlier)/earlier × 100. Compare and choose the largest.
DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||line.w: Choosing the largest absolute rise, which may not be the largest percentage.

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||pie c.m: Angle = share % × 3.6°. Share = angle ÷ 360 × 100. A quantity = share × total.
DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||pie c.w: Using 360 without converting percentages (or vice versa).

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||combi.m: Bars and line use different scales. Convert the margin % into amounts: profit = revenue × margin/100, then compare.
DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||combi.w: Reading the line on the bars' scale.

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||stack.m: The total of a stack is the sum of its segments. Share = segment ÷ total × 100.

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||two p.m: Convert each pie's shares to actual values using that pie's own total, then compare. The percentage shares alone do not compare across different totals.
DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts||two p.w: Comparing the percentages directly when the totals differ.
